blocks.prompt: The Snowflake That Started as Dust
blocks.text: A snowflake does not fall out of the sky ready made. It builds itself on the way down. High in a cold cloud, a tiny speck of dust floats along. Water in the air freezes onto the speck. More water freezes on. The ice grows and grows. It always grows six arms, because that is how water lines up when it turns to ice. The arms grow lacy and wide. When the snowflake gets heavy, it drifts down. It falls slower than you walk. Snow looks white, but a snowflake is really clear. It only looks white because light bounces around inside all that ice.

six
light bounces around inside the ice

3.title: The Snowflake That Started as Dust
3.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 7 to 8
3.intro: Read the passage, then work through each part. You can look back at the passage any time.

meta.templateLabel: The Snowflake That Started as Dust

blocks.prompt: How a Snowflake Builds Itself
blocks.text: Snow does not begin as rain. Rain that freezes on the way down is called sleet, and sleet is just a hard little ball of ice. A real snow crystal never was a raindrop at all. It begins inside a cloud that is colder than freezing. Floating in that cloud is a speck of dust, or pollen, or salt blown up off the sea. Water vapor in the air touches the speck and turns straight into ice, skipping the liquid step altogether. Now there is a seed of ice, and it starts to grow. Water molecules stack onto that seed the only way they fit, which is in six-sided rings. Six sides means six corners, and corners stick out into the damp air, so they collect water fastest. Each corner grows an arm. Each arm sprouts smaller branches. All six arms travel together through the same cold air, so they grow in almost the same pattern at the same time. That is why a snow crystal looks like it was folded and cut from paper. Then it gets heavy, tips over, and falls.

answers: rain that freezes as it falls; it is a hard ball of ice, not a crystal
dust, pollen, or salt from the sea
they stick out furthest into the damp air, so they collect water fastest
(inference: the six arms travel together through the same air, so they grow the same way at the same time)

meta.templateLabel: The Snowflake That Started as Dust

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Shape depends on temperature
Plates near 28F, needles near 23F
The big branching stars grow near 5F

He called snow crystals letters sent from the sky
He grew them on the tip of a rabbit hair

blocks.prompt: Letters Sent From the Sky
blocks.text: Ask most people to draw a snowflake and they will draw a six-pointed star. That shape is real, but it is only one of the shapes snow can take. Snow also falls as flat plates, as hollow columns, as thin needles, and as columns with a plate capping each end like a spool of thread. What decides which shape you get is mostly one thing: the temperature of the air the crystal is growing in. We know this because of a Japanese physicist named Ukichiro Nakaya. In the 1930s, working in the cold of Hokkaido, he grew snow crystals indoors on the tip of a rabbit hair, one at a time, at temperatures he controlled himself. Then he did it again, and again, thousands of times, and mapped what grew at each temperature. Near 28 degrees Fahrenheit he got plates. A few degrees colder he got needles. Near 5 degrees Fahrenheit he got the great branching stars. Colder still, and the crystals went back to plain columns and plates. That map means a snow crystal carries a record of its own journey. It grew arms in the layer where stars grow, plates in the layer where plates grow, and it wandered up and down through the cloud collecting the shape of each layer it passed through. Nakaya said snow crystals are letters sent from the sky. He meant it literally. If you can read the shape, it tells you what the cloud was like.

answers: the temperature of the air it is growing in
he grew them one at a time on a rabbit hair at temperatures he set himself; (inference: outdoors he could not control or know the temperature)

blocks.prompt: No Two Alike, and How We Know
blocks.text: On a January morning in 1885, a nineteen-year-old farmer in Jericho, Vermont, stood in an unheated shed with a camera bolted to a microscope and did something nobody had done before. Wilson Bentley photographed a single snow crystal. He caught the flakes on a board painted black, moved them with a feather, and worked fast, because his own breath could ruin them. Over the next forty-six years he photographed more than five thousand crystals. He never found two that matched. In 1931 he walked home six miles through a blizzard, caught pneumonia, and died a few weeks later. Bentley's line went around the world: no two snowflakes are alike. It is one of the few pieces of folk science that turns out to be almost exactly right, though not for the reason most people assume. A snow crystal is not drawn by a plan. It is built one water molecule at a time, and a large one may contain something like a billion billion of them. Each molecule arrives where it arrives because of the temperature, the humidity, and the wind in that exact spot at that exact instant. Nudge any of those, and the pattern that follows is different. Two crystals would have to take identical paths through a cloud that is never the same twice. The physicist Kenneth Libbrecht, who grows snow crystals in a laboratory at Caltech, adds the honest correction. Very small, very simple crystals, the plain six-sided plates, can and do look identical under a microscope. The claim only holds for the big branching stars. Those have so many possible arrangements that the number of them dwarfs the number of crystals that have ever fallen. So the folk science is safe. Bentley was right, and the reason he was right is that no cloud ever repeats itself.

6.title: The Snowflake That Started as Dust
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Snowflake That Started as Dust

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Ice Ih: frozen water builds in hexagonal rings
A water molecule is a V, about 105 degrees wide
Six arms come from six corners growing fastest
Nakaya mapped shape against temperature in the 1930s
Kenneth Libbrecht grows snow crystals at Caltech
Most crystals that actually fall are lopsided or broken

blocks.prompt: Six Arms, One Rule, and No Repeats
blocks.text: Every snow crystal on Earth obeys one rule, and the rule is set by the shape of a single water molecule. A water molecule is a wide V: one oxygen atom with two hydrogen atoms attached, spread at an angle of about 105 degrees. When water is liquid, the molecules tumble past each other and that angle hardly matters. When water freezes, the molecules lock into a lattice, and the only way that V-shaped piece tiles neatly is in rings of six. Every ordinary ice crystal on this planet is built on hexagons. That is the whole answer to why snowflakes have six arms and not five or eight. The symmetry you see with your eyes at a scale of millimeters is a report from a scale of nanometers, and there is nothing in between deciding it. The rest is growth. A crystal begins on a floating speck of dust or pollen, and water vapor deposits onto it directly, going from gas to solid without ever being liquid. The infant crystal is a tiny hexagonal prism. Its six corners poke furthest out into the vapor, so they gather molecules fastest, and once a corner is ahead it stays ahead. Each corner runs away as an arm. Each arm throws out side branches for the same reason. This runaway is called branching instability, and it is why the finished crystal looks like lace instead of a plain plate. Then why do the six arms match? Because they are not communicating. They are simply six identical structures riding the same crystal through the same air. Temperature and humidity change constantly as the crystal tumbles, and every arm feels each change at the same moment and responds the same way. Symmetry is not coordination. It is six sisters given the same instructions in the same order. And the match is often imperfect. Photographs in books favor the beautiful ones. Most crystals that actually fall are lopsided, broken, clumped together, or crusted with frozen droplets. The strangest part is one we still cannot fully explain. Ukichiro Nakaya, growing crystals in a Hokkaido laboratory in the 1930s, discovered that shape flips with temperature in a way nobody predicted. Near 28 degrees Fahrenheit you get plates. Colder, around 23, you get needles. Colder again, near 5 degrees, you get the enormous branching stars. Colder still, and you are back to columns. The pattern reverses twice across a range you could cross by walking up a hill. Kenneth Libbrecht, who has grown thousands of crystals in a laboratory at Caltech, has spent decades chasing the surface physics behind those flips, and the case is not closed. Which leaves the famous claim. Are no two alike? Strictly, no. Small simple plates can be identical, and researchers have photographed near twins. But a large branching crystal is assembled from roughly a billion billion water molecules, each placed by the exact conditions at the exact instant it arrived. The number of arrangements available to it is larger than the number of crystals that have fallen in the history of the planet. Two matching stars are not forbidden by physics. They are merely so unlikely that the claim is safe forever, which is a more interesting kind of true.
